column1: # Evidence for a country when the text names none and several countries share its postcode form (country inference without a hint).
# Columns: kind, country, value. A country is chosen only when exactly one of the countries that can read the text has evidence, so every row here has to be
# something the other candidates do not write. Words are in the form T2Rules.Key gives (upper case, no accents, periods dropped).
# letters: the letters of the country's language that lie outside Latin-1 (and the German sharp s). Latin-1 letters (a with acute, o with diaeresis, o with stroke, ...) are
#   never evidence: names of every origin carry them. A letter counts for a country only when no other candidate uses it, and a country whose letters do not hold every
#   such letter of the text is not chosen. Sources: the alphabets of the languages, as the UPU sheets and the posts' guides print their example addresses.
# word: a whole word that is a street type or a place word of the language (UPU sheets and the posts' guides: Posten Norge Adressering, Danmarks Adresser Gengivelse af adresse,
#   PostNord Adressering, Omniva, Lietuvos pastas, Magyar Posta, Ceska posta, Poczta Polska, bpost).
# suffix: the end of a street name written as one word (Storgata, Nørregade, Mannerheimintie); the name must be longer than the ending by two letters.
# marked: an abbreviation that is evidence only when a house number of up to four digits follows it directly (Verslo g. 5, Pargi tn 24, Top 5), because alone it could be an initial or a word
#   of another language. after: the same for a word that follows a floor number (3. sal).
# place: a locality that is the whole of a small country's division (the municipalities of Liechtenstein); the Swiss cantons and the UK areas are in their own tables.
# Denmark: vej, gade, allé, stræde, plads, torv (Danmarks Adresser, Gengivelse af adresse); sal for the floor ("3. sal tv").
# Norway: gate, gata, vei, veien, vegen, plass (Posten Norge, Adressering); etasje and inngang for the floor and entrance.
# Sweden: gatan, vägen, gränd, stigen, torg, backen (PostNord, Adressering); lgh is the apartment.
# Finland: katu, tie, kuja, polku, tori, kaari, rinne, puisto (UPU Finland sheet and Posti's examples); krs is the floor (kerros), as. the apartment.
# Estonia: tänav, maantee, puiestee, tee, and the county, rural municipality and village words (UPU Estonia sheet, Omniva).
# Estonia: the towns (linn) and county names in the one-word forms (Harjumaa) are the country's own divisions and nobody else writes them (Statistics Estonia list of towns; Omniva

#   writes the county as maakond or as one word ending in -maa). Towns whose name is also an ordinary word elsewhere (Elva, Turi, Valga, Pussi, Polva, Rapina) are left out. Hyphenated towns (Kohtla-Jarve, Abja-Paluoja) are listed by their first part. poik (lane), valjak (square) and
#   postkast (post office box) are street and delivery words of Omniva.
# Latvia: iela, prospekts, bulvaris, novads, pagasts (the Latvian rules for unified postal addresses).
# Lithuania: gatvė (g.), prospektas (pr.), alėja (al.), kaimas (k.), savivaldybė (sav.) (UPU Lithuania sheet, Lietuvos paštas).
# Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia, Hungary (Poczta Polska, Ceska posta, UPU sheets, Magyar Posta).
# zone: the digits a postcode of the country may start with, where that tells it from a neighbour sharing the form: the first digit of a Czechoslovak postcode names the region of the
#   former federation, 1 to 7 for the Czech lands and 0, 8 and 9 for Slovakia (Wikipedia, Postal codes in the Czech Republic and in Slovakia, retrieved 2026-11-06). zoneonly: the digits
#   that no other country of the shared form starts a postcode with (Sweden's start at 1), so they are evidence.
# The Netherlands writes the Belgian Dutch endings alike, so they are evidence for neither alone.
# German-speaking and neighbouring countries: spellings that belong to one of them (bpost Belgian template, UPU sheets).
# Liechtenstein's eleven municipalities (Gemeinden): the whole of the country's division, so a locality that is one of them is Liechtenstein's.
# Italy and Spain: road words that only one of the countries sharing the five-digit form writes (UPU Italy and Spain sheets, Poste Italiane Standard di composizione indirizzi). Via and
# Calle are not listed: Via is also Spanish and Calle also Mexican, and both are in any American address as well.
# language: the languages a country's word and suffix rows above are written in, where that is not all the languages the country writes (Belgium's endings are Dutch, Luxembourg's
#   Luxembourgish) or where two neighbours understand each other's street words (Danish and Norwegian). A text that holds a word of some language can only be a text of a country
#   that writes that language; without this row a country's rows belong to every language it writes (t2-countries*.tsv).
# lang: a whole word that belongs to a language although no country's evidence rows above list it, or that a language shares with the language the rows give it to (allee and
#   chaussee are also French street types; ulica is Croatian and Slovak as well as Slovenian and Polish; aleja is also Croatian and Slovenian). Street types of the UPU sheets and
#   the posts' guides (La Poste Guide pratique courrier, Correos, CTT, Poczta Polska, Hrvatska posta).
# langsuffix: the same for the end of a street name written as one word; endings under four letters are ignored.
